title: A Career in Whisky Marketing | Craft Beer School
desc: What whisky marketers in India actually do, the rules they work within and the product knowledge that sets the good ones apart.
teaser: In India you cannot advertise whisky directly. Whisky marketing here is the craft of building a brand inside that rule.
standfirst: Whisky marketing looks glamorous from outside: launches, tastings, award ceremonies. Inside, it is a job of brand planning, trade relationships and careful compliance. In India it comes with one rule that shapes everything else.
sections: The rule that shapes the job

Direct advertising of alcohol is not allowed in India. There are no whisky ads on television, no billboards that show a bottle and say buy this. Brands build awareness through other routes: events, bar and restaurant programmes, packaging, digital content within platform and legal limits and the people who pour and recommend the product.

So a whisky marketer here spends less time on mass media and more on everything around it. The rules are interpreted by regulators and courts and they change. Every serious drinks company has a legal or compliance team reviewing campaigns. A marketer who understands the boundaries saves everyone weeks of rework. Our guide to whisky digital marketing within the rules goes further on this.

• Brand manager. Owns one brand or range: its positioning, its pricing tier, its calendar of launches and activations and its budget.
  • Trade marketing. Works with bars, restaurants and retail. Menus, staff training, back bar visibility and promotions where state rules allow them.
  • Brand ambassador. The face of the brand to bartenders and drinkers. Runs tastings, trains staff and tells the brand's story.
  • Digital and content. Social media, websites and content, with age gating and careful wording.
  • Consumer insight. Research and data on who drinks what, where and why.

Entry usually comes through sales, trade marketing or a graduate scheme at a large drinks company. Experience in fast moving consumer goods transfers well.

Plenty of marketers can run a campaign. Fewer can explain why a twelve year old malt tastes the way it does. In whisky, that knowledge is respected by bartenders, journalists and serious drinkers, who can tell when a brand team does not know its own product.

You do not need to be a distiller. You do need to understand the basics well enough to avoid saying something false. Scotch must mature at least three years in oak casks in Scotland. An age statement refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle. For Scotch, single malt means malted barley distilled in pot stills at one distillery. A marketer who calls a blend a single malt, or implies an age the liquid does not have, creates a compliance problem and a credibility problem at once.

Knowing the process also gives you better stories. Cask types, still shapes, the effect of Indian heat on maturation and the choice of barley are all real differences you can talk about honestly. Our guide to how whisky is made covers the whole chain.
Sensory skills help more than people expect

Marketers who can taste properly write better copy and brief agencies better. They can sit in a blending room discussion and follow it. They can tell when a tasting note is invented.

Sensory training is a skill, not a talent. It means learning to nose with a small measure, often around 15 to 25 ml, adding a few drops of water to open the aroma, building a vocabulary and checking it against other tasters. It always means responsible practice: spitting at work tastings, water between samples and never drinking and driving after an event. Many companies run sensory sessions for marketing teams for exactly this reason.
What a good week looks like

A brand manager's week might include a review of depletion data by state, a call with a design agency about a gift pack, a visit to a bar group to agree a menu listing and a compliance check on a social post. Numbers matter. Marketers in drinks companies are measured on volume, value and share, so comfort with a spreadsheet is part of the job.

The work also follows India's festive calendar. Diwali and the year end are peak gifting periods for whisky. Planning for them starts months earlier, because packaging and label approvals take time.

The best brand teams spend time at the distillery. A marketer who has stood next to a spirit still during a run, nosed new make straight from the safe and walked a warehouse in May understands what the brand is selling. That understanding shows in the work.

It also helps with internal politics. Production teams are often wary of marketing claims they consider loose. A marketer who asks the distiller to check a story before it goes out builds trust and avoids embarrassing corrections. Simple rules help: never print a number the production team has not confirmed, never describe a process the distillery does not use and never imply an age or a cask the liquid has not seen.

For marketers in India, it is worth learning what molasses based spirit is too. Much of the volume in the Indian whisky market is built on it. Knowing how it differs from malt or grain whisky helps you position any brand honestly.

Pick three whisky labels from a shop shelf and write down every claim on each one: age, category, cask, region. Then check each claim against what the rules allow and what the words actually mean. If you cannot tell whether a claim is meaningful, that is the knowledge gap worth closing before your first interview.
faqs: Can whisky be advertised in India?
Direct advertising of alcohol is not allowed in India. Brands build awareness through events, trade programmes, packaging and carefully reviewed digital content.
Do whisky marketers need production knowledge?
They do not need to distil, but understanding the process avoids false claims and gives more honest stories to tell.
How do people get into whisky marketing?
Common routes are sales, trade marketing, graduate schemes at drinks companies or consumer goods marketing roles.
